nodes.title: Our score is binary and our gate is a continuous-delta test, so the gate is measuring nothing
nodes.body:
Replayed all 227 recorded rounds from 62 campaigns. 208 carry a score, and there are exactly two distinct values across all of them: 0 (72 rounds) and 1 (136 rounds). Statuses are promoted 114, no-gain 91, interrupted 23, holdout-failed 3. Of 118 (campaign, task) series, only 10 ever show a score that changes between rounds (8.5%).

Why this is the central defect rather than a cosmetic one: the gate is `score - taskBest >= minGain - 1e-9` with minGain 0.05, which is a test of a continuous delta. With a binary score the only reachable margins are 0 and 1, so minGain is either satisfied by 1 (and the gate accepts) or by 0 (and it rejects). The gate therefore collapses to "the verifier passed and it did not pass last time", and the entire statistics discussion — noise floors, sample size, PACE-style deviation — does not apply, because there is no distribution to be noisy. Worse, once a task has ever scored 1, its taskBest is 1 forever, so every later passing patch on that task is judged no-gain and can never be promoted again. That is the local shape of the same bug I already fixed once (bestPriorScore comparing across tasks); it recurs within a task as soon as a task can only score 0 or 1.

The mechanism-level conclusion: the gate wants a graded signal. The verifier already supports it — parseMetrics reads numbers out of stdout via per-name regex patterns, tries[].metrics is threaded through round.js, and every round currently records `metrics: {}`. The infrastructure exists and is never populated, because every eval task in every campaign declares verify:{cmd} and never verify:{metrics}. A task can therefore be made to produce a continuous score for free: parse a coverage percentage, a count of failing assertions, or a timing, and the gate becomes a real comparison.

Limitation: a graded score only helps if the grade is monotone with quality, and a partial-credit metric is exactly where Goodhart damage shows up first. The safe version is a graded signal used only for the promotion comparison, with the binary pass required as a precondition, so no campaign can promote a patch that fails the tests because it improved a proxy.

nodes.title: Binary scoring also explains why the loop converged so fast and then sat still
nodes.body:
44 of 62 campaigns stopped with 0 promotions, and the aggregate promotion rate is 55% (114 of 208 scored rounds) concentrated in the rounds before a task first reaches 1.0. The pattern is consistent with a ceiling: a task whose verifier is `node tests/x.test.mjs` scores 0 until the patch makes it pass and 1 forever after, so each task offers exactly one promotable transition and the campaign's job is to find it once.

That is a defensible design for a spec-satisfaction campaign — the task is literally to make a failing test pass — but it means the loop cannot iterate on quality once the spec passes, which is precisely the "RSI" the plugin claims to do. The ladder above L0 has nothing to climb: L1 and L2 optimise against a signal that has two values.

This reframes the plugin's own roadmap. The missing piece is not a better gate or a better policy, it is a task whose score has a gradient — coverage, mutation score, latency, benchmark accuracy, lint debt — plus a hard pass/fail precondition so the gradient can never buy a worse-but-greener patch. With such a task the existing machinery (bestPriorScore, minGain, plateau detection, lesson attribution) becomes meaningful for the first time, and its weaknesses become measurable instead of theoretical.

edges.note: The PACE-style statistical critique assumes a noisy continuous score; ours is binary, which is a different and worse failure.
A binary score makes the acceptor degenerate rather than noisy.
Explains the observed plateau as a ceiling in the signal, not a plateau in the search.
Follows from the binary score being unclimbable after first success.
